concepts.name: Constitutional Basis of Subordinate Courts: Articles 233–237
key_dimensions: Exact articles governing district courts vs. subordinate courts and which article covers which
Distinction between 'district courts' and 'courts subordinate thereto' — scope and hierarchy
Why these provisions fall under Chapter VI of Part VI (applicability to states only, not Union Territories)
UPSC trap: Article 237 extends provisions to magistrates — overlap with executive magistracy

concepts.name: Appointment of District Judges: Article 233
key_dimensions: Role of Governor vs. High Court — who appoints, who consults (mandatory consultation vs. concurrence)
Two categories: persons already in judicial service vs. persons at the Bar — different eligibility conditions
UPSC trap: 'Consultation' with High Court under Article 233 vs. 'concurrence' under Article 217 for HC judges
Rameshwar Dayal case and subsequent SC rulings on binding nature of HC recommendation

concepts.name: Definition and Scope of 'District Judge' under Article 236
key_dimensions: Inclusive definition under Article 236(a): covers City Civil Court judge, Additional District Judge, Sessions Judge, Additional Sessions Judge, Chief Judge of Small Cause Court, etc.
UPSC trap: Sessions Judge and District Judge can be the same person — dual capacity under CrPC
Exclusion of judicial officers below the rank of district judge from Article 233 protection
Why the definition matters for service protections and appointment procedures

concepts.name: Posting, Promotion, and Transfer of District Judges: Article 233 and 235 Interface
key_dimensions: Article 233 governs appointment; Article 235 governs control — different authority for each
Governor acts on the advice of High Court for transfers and postings of district judges
UPSC trap: Control under Article 235 vests in High Court, NOT Governor — direct HC control
Controversy: Whether 'control' includes disciplinary proceedings — SC ruling in State of West Bengal v. Nripendra Nath Bagchi

concepts.name: Control of High Court over Subordinate Courts: Article 235
key_dimensions: Scope of 'control': posting, promotion, leave, and discipline of judicial officers (not district judges alone)
Distinction between superintendence (Article 227) and control (Article 235) — different scope and depth
UPSC trap: Article 235 control does NOT extend to ministerial staff of subordinate courts
Whether control under Article 235 is exclusive — interplay with state government's role in service conditions

concepts.name: Superintendence of High Courts over Subordinate Courts: Article 227
key_dimensions: Article 227 vs. Article 235: superintendence is broader (includes all courts including tribunals) while Article 235 is narrower
Revisional and supervisory jurisdiction — HC can call for records, make general rules, prescribe forms
UPSC trap: Article 227 extends to ALL courts AND tribunals within territorial jurisdiction, unlike Article 235
Limitations: HC cannot act as appellate court under Article 227; it is supervisory only — Waryam Singh case

concepts.name: Recruitment to Judicial Service below District Judge: Article 234
key_dimensions: State Public Service Commission + High Court consultation mandatory — both must be involved
UPSC trap: For district judges (Article 233), only HC consultation required; for below district judge (Article 234), SPSC + HC both required
Governor makes rules but cannot exclude either HC or SPSC from the process
Judicial independence rationale: Why HC is given a role in recruitment even at lower levels

concepts.name: Hierarchy of Civil Courts at the District Level
key_dimensions: Hierarchy: District Court → Civil Judge (Senior Division) → Civil Judge (Junior Division) — varies by state legislation
Pecuniary jurisdiction thresholds differ by state — not uniform across India (UPSC trap on 'uniform' claims)
Original vs. appellate jurisdiction at each tier within civil court hierarchy
Small Causes Courts in Presidency towns (Mumbai, Chennai) — special status, not part of regular hierarchy

concepts.name: Hierarchy of Criminal Courts: CrPC Section 6 and the Court Structure
key_dimensions: Hierarchy under CrPC: Sessions Court → Chief Judicial Magistrate → Judicial Magistrate First Class → Judicial Magistrate Second Class → Executive Magistrate (separate track)
UPSC trap: Executive Magistrates are NOT part of the judicial hierarchy — they are revenue/administrative officers under the state
Sessions Judge and Additional Sessions Judge — power to award any sentence including death (subject to HC confirmation)
Chief Metropolitan Magistrate in metropolitan areas vs. Chief Judicial Magistrate in other areas

concepts.name: Sessions Court: Jurisdiction, Constitution, and Special Features
key_dimensions: Established by state government under CrPC; every sessions division must have a Sessions Court
Sessions Judge appointed by High Court — direct HC appointment, unlike lower magistrates
Original jurisdiction (sessions triable offences) + appellate jurisdiction over magistrate courts
UPSC trap: Sessions Court can confirm death sentences but execution requires HC confirmation — two-step process

concepts.name: Executive Magistracy vs. Judicial Magistracy: Separation and Overlap
key_dimensions: CrPC 1973 mandated separation of judiciary from executive — all states required to implement
Executive Magistrates: District Magistrate, Sub-Divisional Magistrate, etc. — handle preventive jurisdiction (Section 144, 107 CrPC)
UPSC trap: Executive Magistrates still exercise quasi-judicial powers (Section 144 orders, externment) — not purely administrative
Article 237 allows states to apply HC-service provisions to magistrates — blurring the separation in some contexts

concepts.name: Family Courts: Establishment, Jurisdiction, and Special Features
key_dimensions: Family Courts Act 1984 — mandatory establishment in cities with population over 1 million, optional elsewhere
Jurisdiction: matrimonial disputes, custody, maintenance, adoption — civil in nature, not criminal
UPSC trap: Family Courts are NOT part of the regular civil court hierarchy — they are specialized courts with exclusive jurisdiction
No right to legal representation as a matter of course — court can refuse lawyers to promote conciliation

concepts.name: Fast Track Courts and Special Courts: Constitutional and Statutory Basis
key_dimensions: Fast Track Courts established by 11th Finance Commission recommendation — not constitutionally mandated
Special Courts under various statutes: POCSO, SC/ST Act, NIA Act — different parent legislation, different procedures
UPSC trap: Fast Track Courts for rape/POCSO cases (Criminal Law Amendment 2013 and 2018) vs. general FTCs — different mandate
Accountability gap: Fast Track Courts lack permanent statutory basis in many states — state discretion issue

concepts.name: Gram Nyayalayas: Constitutional Vision vs. Statutory Reality
key_dimensions: Gram Nyayalayas Act 2008 — to establish courts at intermediate panchayat level for grassroots justice
Nyayadhikari (presiding officer) is a First Class Judicial Magistrate appointed by state government in consultation with HC
UPSC trap: Establishment is NOT mandatory — states 'may' establish, leading to poor implementation (only ~500 of 5000+ mandated)
Jurisdiction: both civil and criminal (petty offences) — mobile court concept; can sit in villages

concepts.name: Lok Adalats: Legal Status, Jurisdiction, and Binding Nature
key_dimensions: Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 — awards of Lok Adalat are deemed decrees of civil courts, executable as such
UPSC trap: Lok Adalat award is FINAL — no appeal lies to any court (only writ jurisdiction under Articles 226/227 available)
Permanent Lok Adalats under 2002 amendment — can adjudicate (not just conciliate) in public utility service disputes
No court fees payable; if case settled, court fees refunded — incentive structure for settlement

concepts.name: Tribunals vs. Subordinate Courts: Distinctions and Overlaps
key_dimensions: Tribunals: creatures of statute, adjudicate specific subject matters; subordinate courts: part of constitutional judicial hierarchy
Article 323A and 323B: constitutional basis for administrative and other tribunals — substitutes HC original jurisdiction
UPSC trap: SC in L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held tribunals cannot exclude HC jurisdiction under Articles 226/227 — they are supplemental, not substitutes
Difference in appointment: tribunal members appointed by executive; subordinate court judges — HC plays mandatory role

concepts.name: Cadre Management and All-India Judicial Service (AIJS): Proposal and Controversy
key_dimensions: Article 312 allows Parliament to create AIJS — analogous to IAS/IPS for district judiciary
Arguments for: uniformity, merit-based selection, reduce HC dominance in appointments
UPSC trap: AIJS would cover only District Judges and above — NOT the entire subordinate judiciary; requires two-third majority of Rajya Sabha and state concurrence
Opposition from High Courts and many states — federalism concern and judicial independence argument

concepts.name: Pendency Crisis in Subordinate Courts: Structural and Constitutional Dimensions
key_dimensions: Over 3.5 crore cases pending in district/subordinate courts — structural underfunding and judge vacancy issue
UPSC trap: Judge-to-population ratio — India has ~21 judges per million (Law Commission recommended 50 per million in 120th report)
Constitutional responsibility: Who is accountable — state government (infrastructure), HC (control/posting), Centre (funding via 13th/14th FC norms)?
Section 309 CrPC (day-to-day trial) vs. ground reality — gap between law and implementation

concepts.name: Nyaya Panchayats and Village Courts: Historical and Contemporary Relevance
key_dimensions: Directive Principle — Article 40 directs organization of village panchayats; some states extend quasi-judicial functions
UPSC trap: Nyaya Panchayats are NOT part of the formal judicial hierarchy under CrPC or Constitution — they are statutory creations of state legislation
Distinction from Gram Nyayalayas (under 2008 Act) — Gram Nyayalayas are proper courts presided by magistrates; Nyaya Panchayats are lay bodies
Controversy: Caste bias in village-level adjudication — khap panchayat orders vs. formal Nyaya Panchayat proceedings

concepts.name: Interplay Between State Legislature and High Court in Shaping Subordinate Court Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: State legislature can alter pecuniary jurisdiction, territorial jurisdiction of subordinate courts through legislation
UPSC trap: State cannot legislate to REMOVE HC's power of superintendence (Article 227) or revisional jurisdiction — constitutional floor cannot be legislated away
High Court's power to make rules (Article 227(3)) vs. state's power to prescribe court fees, procedures — potential conflict
Recent example: States creating new court tiers (e.g., Commercial Courts Act 2015 — concurrent jurisdiction issue)
